questions.prompt: Describe the three core components of the iOS code signing triangle and how they work together.
questions.modelAnswer: The code signing triangle consists of a Certificate, an App ID, and a Provisioning Profile. The Certificate proves the developer identity using public-key cryptography. The App ID uniquely identifies the app and enables specific capabilities like Push Notifications. The Provisioning Profile acts as the binding glue, combining the certificate, the App ID with entitlements, and allowed test device identifiers.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the three components as Certificate, App ID (Bundle ID), and Provisioning Profile.
Explains how the provisioning profile binds identity, capabilities, and device eligibility together.

questions.prompt: Explain why development provisioning profiles require registered device UDIDs while App Store profiles do not.
questions.modelAnswer: Development provisioning profiles are designed for team debugging on specific hardware. Apple restricts installation to explicitly registered test device UDIDs to prevent unauthorized distribution. App Store distribution profiles omit device UDIDs because Apple re-signs the final binary with Apple FairPlay DRM, permitting installation on any consumer device worldwide.

rubric.criterion: Explains development profiles restrict installation to registered hardware test devices.
Explains App Store profiles omit UDIDs because Apple signs releases for universal customer installation.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between `CFBundleShortVersionString` and `CFBundleVersion`, and state the rule for uploading new builds.
questions.modelAnswer: `CFBundleShortVersionString` is the public marketing version displayed on the App Store, such as 2.1.0. `CFBundleVersion` is the internal build number used by App Store Connect to sequence uploads. When uploading a new build for the same marketing version, `CFBundleVersion` must be strictly higher than the previous upload, or the upload will be rejected.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates public marketing version (CFBundleShortVersionString) from internal build number (CFBundleVersion).
Explains that each new upload requires an increased build number to pass validation.

questions.prompt: What is Phased Release on the App Store, how does the 7-day schedule work, and why is it useful?
questions.modelAnswer: Phased Release is an App Store release option that rolls out an update to automatic-update users over seven days. The rollout starts at 1% on Day 1. It increases to 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, and reaches 100% on Day 7. It is useful because it allows teams to detect unforeseen production crashes early and pause the rollout before all users are affected.

rubric.criterion: Describes the 7-day progressive rollout percentages starting at 1% and reaching 100% by Day 7.
Explains that phased rollout limits blast radius by allowing teams to catch and pause bugs early.

questions.prompt: Compare Internal Testing and External Testing in TestFlight, focusing on tester capacity and review requirements.
questions.modelAnswer: Internal Testing supports up to 100 App Store Connect team members. Builds are available immediately after server processing with no Apple review required. External Testing supports up to 10,000 public testers invited by email or public links. External testing requires Beta App Review approval from Apple for the first build of each new marketing version before testers can access it.

rubric.criterion: States internal testing has a 100-member limit and requires no Apple review.
States external testing supports up to 10,000 testers and requires Beta App Review for version builds.
